newsitem.title: UK: UK's Major blames IRA for Grand National alert.
newsitem.headline: UK's Major blames IRA for Grand National alert.

text.p: The Grand National horse race, one of Britain's great annual sporting events, was abandoned on Saturday because of a bomb alert that Prime Minister John Major blamed on the Irish Republican Army (IRA).

The Aintree race course near the northwestern English port city of Liverpool was evacuated about 30 minutes before the 3:45 p.m. (1445 GMT) scheduled start of the four-and-a-half mile (7.2 km) steeplechase after police said they received two coded warnings of bombs at the sprawling track.

Officials abandoned racing for the rest of the day. A decision would be taken on Sunday on when to re-schedule the main race. Police said it was too early to say whether it could be run on Monday as the course was still being searched.

Police said crowds outside the course would not be allowed in on Saturday to retrieve cars inside the perimeter, a decision that would trap thousands of in the area for the night. Local authorities were opening sports halls and leisure centres to accommodate them.
Security forces carried out two controlled explosions at the race course after finding several suspect packages following the evacuation and said more of the controlled blasts were likely.

There was no immediate claim of responsibility for the alerts. But Major, who is in the midst of campaigning for a May 1 general election, issued a swift statement condemning the IRA, which is fighting for an end to British rule in Northern Ireland, as "cynical and detestable."

Security sources believe the IRA is trying to force Northern Ireland on to the campaign agenda, where it has received scant attention. Saturday's bomb alert followed massive disruption on motorways in central England on Thursday after the discovery of two IRA bombs on road bridges.
Bomb warnings, also believed to be the work of the IRA, disrupted rail and underground services in London on Friday at the height of the evening rush-hour.

Major said on Saturday: "I am appalled that the IRA seem to be threatening hundreds of thousands of people and causing such disprution. This is further demonstration of their contempt and disregard for the lives and interest of ordinary people."
"The IRA's campaign is cynical and detestable. They must know that this can only harden our resolve never to make concessions to terrorists," he added.
Opposition Labour Party leader Tony Blair, whose party is well ahead of Major's Conservative Party in public opinion polls, said a "contemptible" campaign by the IRA had wrecked the Grand National.
"It has been deliberately ruined by a cynical terrorist act, perpetrated by people whose intention is to introduce terror into the election campaign," he said.

Aintree spokesman Nigel Payne told reporters on Saturday: "The police have received two coded bomb warnings, and they felt it was the most appropriate thing to evacuate the entire racecourse. From our point of view, the safety of spectators is the most paramount thing."
Jockey Carl Llewellyn, due to ride outsider Camelot King in the big race, described the situation as sick. "Whoever did this are not sportsmen," he said.
Jenny Pitman, trainer of such past winners as Corbiere and Royal Athlete, called for the horses to be returned to the starting gate and the race to be run.
About 100 horses were believed to have been left in their stables when racegoers and officials were evacuated.

IRA strategy for years has been to attack the British mainland to force British public opinion to put pressure on government to find a solution to the 28-year Northern Ireland conflict, which has cost billions of pounds in damage and disruption and 3,200 lives.
Four years ago the Grand National ended in turmoil in different circumstances after two false starts led to the race being declared void.
